Title: Labour leadership: Jeremy Corbyn makes it onto the ballot

Jeremy Corbyn has secured his place on the leadership ballot.
Nominations for Labour leader closed at 12.00 today. Candidates needed the backing of 35 MPs to make it through to the next round. This morning Corbyn was the only person out of the four to throw their name into the ring not to have reached this threshold and it was unclear whether he’d be able to secure this level of support.
However, MPs came out to nominate him right up until the 12.00 deadline. With a vocal online campaign from Labour activists calling for Corbyn to remain in the contest, many MPs who nominated him said they did so to ensure that the debate stayed as broad as possible.
It seems that the last person to nominate him was Andrew Smith MP for Oxford East. Others who also came out to back Corbyn in the last half an hour before nominations closed include Jon Cruddas, Gareth Thomas and Margaret Beckett.

Title: So, who are the 'moronic MPs' who nominated Jeremy Corbyn for the Labour leadership contest? | The Independent
Chunks: 0,1,2
The MPs who allowed Jeremy Corbyn to enter the Labour leadership contest so the party could "have a debate" are morons, according to a former adviser to Tony Blair.
Mr Corbyn, who is on course to become Labour leader according to the first public poll of those eligible to vote, scraped onto the ballot paper by winning the backing of 35 MPs - the minimum number of nominations needed to enter the race.
Some admitted nominating Mr Corbyn to ensure the contest represented the full spectrum of voices in the party and hoped members would dismiss the crazy views of the left in favour of a more mainstream candidate.
But John McTernan, who advised Mr Blair during his time as Prime Minister, blamed them for the "disastrous" poll, which gave Mr Corbyn an astonishing 17 per cent lead over the second-placed candidate, Andy Burnham.
In a blistering attack, Mr McTernan told BBC Two _Newsnight:_ “The moronic MPs who nominated Jeremy Corbyn to ‘have a debate’ need their heads felt. They should be ashamed of themselves. They’re morons.”

Jeremy Corbyn has secured his place on the leadership ballot.
Nominations for Labour leader closed at 12.00 today. Candidates needed the backing of 35 MPs to make it through to the next round. This morning Corbyn was the only person out of the four to throw their name into the ring not to have reached this threshold and it was unclear whether he’d be able to secure this level of support.
However, MPs came out to nominate him right up until the 12.00 deadline. With a vocal online campaign from Labour activists calling for Corbyn to remain in the contest, many MPs who nominated him said they did so to ensure that the debate stayed as broad as possible.
It seems that the last person to nominate him was Andrew Smith MP for Oxford East. Others who also came out to back Corbyn in the last half an hour before nominations closed include Jon Cruddas, Gareth Thomas and Margaret Beckett.
This means the Labour leadership contest is a four person race between: Andy Burnham, Yvette Cooper, Jeremy Corbyn and Liz Kendall.
Here’s the full list of who nominated whom:

Title: Labour leadership: Jeremy Corbyn makes it onto the ballot
Chunks: 0,1,2
Jeremy Corbyn has secured his place on the leadership ballot.
Nominations for Labour leader closed at 12.00 today. Candidates needed the backing of 35 MPs to make it through to the next round. This morning Corbyn was the only person out of the four to throw their name into the ring not to have reached this threshold and it was unclear whether he’d be able to secure this level of support.
However, MPs came out to nominate him right up until the 12.00 deadline. With a vocal online campaign from Labour activists calling for Corbyn to remain in the contest, many MPs who nominated him said they did so to ensure that the debate stayed as broad as possible.
It seems that the last person to nominate him was Andrew Smith MP for Oxford East. Others who also came out to back Corbyn in the last half an hour before nominations closed include Jon Cruddas, Gareth Thomas and Margaret Beckett.
This means the Labour leadership contest is a four person race between: Andy Burnham, Yvette Cooper, Jeremy Corbyn and Liz Kendall.

Title: Keir Starmer’s Labour leadership bid wins backing of MPs and Unison
Chunks: 0,1
Keir Starmer’s Labour leadership campaign has received a boost after he won the backing of the UK’s biggest trade union, Unison, and became the first person to get more than the 22 MPs required to become a candidate.
The shadow Brexit secretary is all but certain to be one of the names put to a vote of the Labour membership, after Dave Prentis, the Unison general secretary, declared the union would be endorsing him.
In another statement soon afterwards, Prentis said his union would back Angela Rayner to be the deputy leader, cementing her status as the favourite to win that role.
“This is a pivotal time for Labour,” Prentis said. “We believe – if elected by the membership – Keir Starmer would be a leader to bring the party together and win back the trust of the thousands of voters who deserted Labour last month.
“Keir has a clear vision to get Labour back to the winning ways of the past. He is best placed to take on Boris Johnson, hold his government to account and ensure Labour can return to power and once more change working people’s lives for the better.”
On Rayner, Prentis said she had “a long association” with Unison as a member and a former union rep, adding: “Angie’s popularity across the party means she is the right person to handle the challenges of this job.”
Starmer is thought to have about 26 backers, including Ben Bradshaw, David Lammy, and Debbie Abrahams. Jo Stevens, the former shadow Welsh secretary, set out her reasons for backing him in a blog, saying she asked every voter at the election who had reservations about Jeremy Corbyn who the leader should be. “With the exception of one person, the answer every time was Keir Starmer,” she said.
Rebecca Long Bailey, who is backed by a number of Corbyn allies, has at least 12 supportive MPs, from the party chairman, Ian Lavery, to John McDonnell, who said she would be a “superb” choice. Diane Abbott, the shadow home secretary, declared her support for Long Bailey on Wednesday.
Long Bailey also appears to be gaining big support among the 2019 new intake, including Navendu Mishra, Kate Osborne, Kim Johnson, Apsana Begum and Paula Barker.

Jess Phillips, on the Corbyn-sceptic side of the party, also has at least 11 MPs. One of her supporters, Wes Streeting, said she was “the person who captures the public’s imagination”. Her campaign said it was “confident we have the nominations needed to make it through to the next stage of this important contest”.
Lisa Nandy, who impressed many undecided MPs at a hustings on Tuesday night with her diagnosis of what went wrong at the election, has seven declared supporters. She won the backing on Wednesday of Jon Ashworth, the shadow health secretary, who said Nandy was the “authentic leftwing voice” for the leadership.
“Lisa brings a distinctive pitch to this campaign because many of the problems we’ve been facing in our more traditional seats, she’s been warning about that for some time,” he said.
The other two candidates – Clive Lewis and Emily Thornberry – have only one public endorsement each so far from Rachael Maskell and Fabian Hamilton respectively, suggesting they may struggle to make the ballot paper.
Lewis, a pro-European on the left of the party, announced on Wednesday that he would seek to work with the Green party if elected leader on a two-year project “to build the ideas, movements and democratic structures that would enable a green new deal to be introduced”.
“I have long been committed to a more plural politics and this is a tangible way of delivering on that commitment,” he said. “We need a new politics of collaboration and openness as the building blocks of the political forces and practices necessary for progressives to take power nationally by 2024 at the latest.”
If candidates win enough support among MPs, they will then have to get the backing of three affiliates, including two trade unions, or about 33 constituency Labour parties. Starmer is thought likely to meet that threshold with the Unison backing as well as local party nominations, while Long Bailey is also expected to meet the test by gaining the support of Unite and possibly other unions, as well as local parties.
However, it looks potentially more challenging for the other candidates to meet the test. After clearing those hurdles, the remaining candidates will face a vote of the party’s 500,000 or so members, any registered supporters who sign up, members of affiliated societies and trade union members.

Keir Starmer’s Labour leadership campaign has received a boost after he won the backing of the UK’s biggest trade union, Unison, and became the first person to get more than the 22 MPs required to become a candidate.
The shadow Brexit secretary is all but certain to be one of the names put to a vote of the Labour membership, after Dave Prentis, the Unison general secretary, declared the union would be endorsing him.
In another statement soon afterwards, Prentis said his union would back Angela Rayner to be the deputy leader, cementing her status as the favourite to win that role.
“This is a pivotal time for Labour,” Prentis said. “We believe – if elected by the membership – Keir Starmer would be a leader to bring the party together and win back the trust of the thousands of voters who deserted Labour last month.
“Keir has a clear vision to get Labour back to the winning ways of the past. He is best placed to take on Boris Johnson, hold his government to account and ensure Labour can return to power and once more change working people’s lives for the better.”
On Rayner, Prentis said she had “a long association” with Unison as a member and a former union rep, adding: “Angie’s popularity across the party means she is the right person to handle the challenges of this job.”
Starmer is thought to have about 26 backers, including Ben Bradshaw, David Lammy, and Debbie Abrahams. Jo Stevens, the former shadow Welsh secretary, set out her reasons for backing him in a blog, saying she asked every voter at the election who had reservations about Jeremy Corbyn who the leader should be. “With the exception of one person, the answer every time was Keir Starmer,” she said.
Rebecca Long Bailey, who is backed by a number of Corbyn allies, has at least 12 supportive MPs, from the party chairman, Ian Lavery, to John McDonnell, who said she would be a “superb” choice. Diane Abbott, the shadow home secretary, declared her support for Long Bailey on Wednesday.
Long Bailey also appears to be gaining big support among the 2019 new intake, including Navendu Mishra, Kate Osborne, Kim Johnson, Apsana Begum and Paula Barker.

Jess Phillips, on the Corbyn-sceptic side of the party, also has at least 11 MPs. One of her supporters, Wes Streeting, said she was “the person who captures the public’s imagination”. Her campaign said it was “confident we have the nominations needed to make it through to the next stage of this important contest”.
Lisa Nandy, who impressed many undecided MPs at a hustings on Tuesday night with her diagnosis of what went wrong at the election, has seven declared supporters. She won the backing on Wednesday of Jon Ashworth, the shadow health secretary, who said Nandy was the “authentic leftwing voice” for the leadership.
“Lisa brings a distinctive pitch to this campaign because many of the problems we’ve been facing in our more traditional seats, she’s been warning about that for some time,” he said.
The other two candidates – Clive Lewis and Emily Thornberry – have only one public endorsement each so far from Rachael Maskell and Fabian Hamilton respectively, suggesting they may struggle to make the ballot paper.
Lewis, a pro-European on the left of the party, announced on Wednesday that he would seek to work with the Green party if elected leader on a two-year project “to build the ideas, movements and democratic structures that would enable a green new deal to be introduced”.
“I have long been committed to a more plural politics and this is a tangible way of delivering on that commitment,” he said. “We need a new politics of collaboration and openness as the building blocks of the political forces and practices necessary for progressives to take power nationally by 2024 at the latest.”
If candidates win enough support among MPs, they will then have to get the backing of three affiliates, including two trade unions, or about 33 constituency Labour parties. Starmer is thought likely to meet that threshold with the Unison backing as well as local party nominations, while Long Bailey is also expected to meet the test by gaining the support of Unite and possibly other unions, as well as local parties.
However, it looks potentially more challenging for the other candidates to meet the test. After clearing those hurdles, the remaining candidates will face a vote of the party’s 500,000 or so members, any registered supporters who sign up, members of affiliated societies and trade union members.

Rt. Hon. Margaret Beckett MP is a British Labour Party politician who is the Member of Parliament for the constituency of Derby South.
Mrs Beckett was first elected to Parliament in 1974 and held junior positions in the governments of Harold Wilson and James Callaghan. She lost her seat in 1979 but returned to the House of Commons in 1983 and became a senior member of the Labour Party. She was elected Deputy Leader of the Labour Party in 1992 and was briefly its leader in 1994 following the premature death of John Smith, the first woman to occupy either role.
After Labour’s victory in the 1997 general election, Mrs Beckett became a member of Tony Blair’s Cabinet. Initially the President of the Board of Trade, she was later the Leader of the House of Commons and Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. In 2006, Mrs Beckett was appointed British Foreign Secretary, making her the first woman to hold the position, and, after Margaret Thatcher, the second woman to hold one of the Great Offices of State.
Margaret Beckett is currently a member of the Top Level Group of UK Parliamentarians for Multilateral Nuclear Disarmament and Non-Proliferation.

Rt. Hon. Margaret Beckett MP is a British Labour Party politician who is the Member of Parliament for the constituency of Derby South.
Mrs Beckett was first elected to Parliament in 1974 and held junior positions in the governments of Harold Wilson and James Callaghan. She lost her seat in 1979 but returned to the House of Commons in 1983 and became a senior member of the Labour Party. She was elected Deputy Leader of the Labour Party in 1992 and was briefly its leader in 1994 following the premature death of John Smith, the first woman to occupy either role.
After Labour’s victory in the 1997 general election, Mrs Beckett became a member of Tony Blair’s Cabinet. Initially the President of the Board of Trade, she was later the Leader of the House of Commons and Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. In 2006, Mrs Beckett was appointed British Foreign Secretary, making her the first woman to hold the position, and, after Margaret Thatcher, the second woman to hold one of the Great Offices of State.
Margaret Beckett is currently a member of the Top Level Group of UK Parliamentarians for Multilateral Nuclear Disarmament and Non-Proliferation.

**Clive Stanley Efford** (born 10 July 1958) is a British Labour Party politician who has been the Member of Parliament (MP) for Eltham and Chislehurst, previously Eltham, since 1997.
Efford was born in London and educated at Walworth School and Southwark College. He went on to win the seat at the ensuing general elections in 2001, 2005 and 2010, with his majority declining after each until the 2015 general election and increased further in 2017. He made his maiden speech in the House of Commons on 25 June 1997.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-3)

**Clive Stanley Efford** (born 10 July 1958) is a British Labour Party politician who has been the Member of Parliament (MP) for Eltham and Chislehurst, previously Eltham, since 1997.
Efford was born in London and educated at Walworth School and Southwark College. He worked in his family jewellery business, until he completed The Knowledge and qualified as London taxi driver in 1987. In 1986, he became an elected councillor in the London Borough of Greenwich, and continued in both these occupations until being elected to Parliament in 1997._[citation needed_]

Efford was first elected to Greenwich Council in 1986 for the Eltham Well Hall Ward.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-electionsCentre-2) He was re-elected in 1990 and 1994, becoming the Labour Group Chief Whip in 1990.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-electionsCentre-2) He did not seek re-election in 1998.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-electionsCentre-2)
After first contesting the seat of Eltham at the 1992 general election, he successfully won the seat five years later in 1997. He went on to win the seat at the ensuing general elections in 2001, 2005 and 2010, with his majority declining after each until the 2015 general election and increased further in 2017. He retained his seat in the 2024 general election despite boundary changes unfavourable to the Labour Party.
He made his maiden speech in the House of Commons on 25 June 1997.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-3)
In Parliament, he has served on a number of Select committees, including being a member of the Transport Select Committee from 2001 to 2008. In 2003, he was one of the Labour MPs who rebelled against the government and voted against UK involvement in the Iraq War. In 2005, Efford was responsible for the reformation of the previously defunct Tribune Group, though unlike its previous incarnation, membership was restricted to backbench Labour MPs.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-4) In 2008, he became the parliamentary private secretary to Housing MinisterMargaret Beckett, later becoming the PPS to John Healey in the same role from 2009 to 2010._[citation needed_]

He was one of the first MPs to declare his support for Ed Miliband, the successful candidate, in the 2010 Labour leadership election. Miliband subsequently appointed him to the Opposition Front Bench in 2011 as a Shadow Home Office Minister under new Shadow Home SecretaryYvette Cooper. In the reshuffle of October 2011, he became the Shadow Minister for Sport.
Clive Efford was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate Jeremy Corbyn as a candidate in the Labour leadership election of 2015[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-5) and he retained his position in Corbyn's shadow cabinet. He resigned from Corbyn's shadow cabinet following a large number of resignations from the Labour front bench on 28 June 2016._[citation needed_] He supported Owen Smith in the failed attempt to replace Jeremy Corbyn in the 2016 Labour leadership election.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-6)
Efford was shortlisted for the Grassroot Diplomat Initiative Award in 2015 for his work on National Health Service Bill, and he remains in the directory of the Grassroot Diplomat Who's Who publication.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-7)
Efford relaunched the Tribune Group of MPs in April 2017, aiming to reconnect with traditional Labour voters while also appealing to the centre ground.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-observer-20170402-8)
Efford endorsed Keir Starmer in the 2020 Labour leadership election.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Efford#cite_note-9)
In August 2025 Efford was a founder member of Mainstream (political organisation) described as a soft left pressure group within the Labour Party.

## Parliamentary career
In October 2016, Huq was appointed as a member of the Shadow Home Affairs team in the Labour Party's frontbench in Parliament. She is Shadow Home Office Minister for Crime Prevention.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon6-38) Huq led from the frontbench on the bill before the House of Commons to equalise Civil Partnerships to include heterosexual couples.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-chiswickherald1-39)

## Parliamentary career
In April 2017, the Green Party decided not to contest her seat in the next general election, commenting, "By and large we quite like Rupa. She has made quite prominent statements on proportional representation and Heathrow, as well as climate change and environmental issues in regards to Brexit."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-independent3-40) In May 2017, Vince Cable commented how he gave Huq a lift home from a joint speaking engagement, saying, "We talked for a couple of hours, and it was very clear that on almost every issue our views were almost identical. And so I would find it difficult to vote against somebody like that, and I hope that our people around the country are discriminating and think and act in a constructive way."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-chiswickherald2-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-spectator2-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph4-43) At the snap 2017 general election, Huq was re-elected as MP for Ealing Central and Acton with an increased vote share of 59.7% and an increased majority of 13,807 votes.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon7-47)
At the 2019 general election, Huq was again re-elected, with a decreased vote share of 51.3% and a decreased majority of 13,300 votes.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-48)

## Parliamentary career
Huq was appointed vice-chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Music Group and All-Party Parliamentary on Crossrail. She chairs the All-Party Parliamentary Group on London, with specific reference to planning and the built environment.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbwhoswho-15) In June 2020 Huq joined the Panel of Chairs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-49) She has been a member of the Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee since March 2022.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-50)
In August 2022, Huq was re-selected as the Labour candidate for Ealing Central and Acton at the 2024 general election.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-51)
In a debate with the UK Parliament House of Commons in March 2024, Huq recognized the expulsion of Armenians from Nagorno-Karabakh as ethnic cleansing, noted the erasure and destruction of Armenian churches and crosses, criticized the UK's dependency on oil for "pull[ing] the strings", expressed support for the UK recognition of the Armenian genocide, and strongly urged the House to provide more assistance to the Armenian refugees.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-52)
In June 2015, she was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate Jeremy Corbyn as a candidate in the Labour leadership election,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman3-53) although she later supported Yvette Cooper.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph3-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman4-55)
Huq supported Owen Smith in his unsuccessful attempt to replace Corbyn in the 2016 Labour Party leadership election.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-56)

## Parliamentary career
In April 2017, the Green Party decided not to contest her seat in the next general election, commenting, "By and large we quite like Rupa. She has made quite prominent statements on proportional representation and Heathrow, as well as climate change and environmental issues in regards to Brexit."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-independent3-40) In May 2017, Vince Cable commented how he gave Huq a lift home from a joint speaking engagement, saying, "We talked for a couple of hours, and it was very clear that on almost every issue our views were almost identical. And so I would find it difficult to vote against somebody like that, and I hope that our people around the country are discriminating and think and act in a constructive way."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-chiswickherald2-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-spectator2-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph4-43) At the snap 2017 general election, Huq was re-elected as MP for Ealing Central and Acton with an increased vote share of 59.7% and an increased majority of 13,807 votes.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon7-47)
At the 2019 general election, Huq was again re-elected, with a decreased vote share of 51.3% and a decreased majority of 13,300 votes.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-48)

## Parliamentary career
Huq was appointed vice-chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Music Group and All-Party Parliamentary on Crossrail. She chairs the All-Party Parliamentary Group on London, with specific reference to planning and the built environment.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbwhoswho-15) In June 2020 Huq joined the Panel of Chairs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-49) She has been a member of the Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee since March 2022.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-50)
In August 2022, Huq was re-selected as the Labour candidate for Ealing Central and Acton at the 2024 general election.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-51)
In a debate with the UK Parliament House of Commons in March 2024, Huq recognized the expulsion of Armenians from Nagorno-Karabakh as ethnic cleansing, noted the erasure and destruction of Armenian churches and crosses, criticized the UK's dependency on oil for "pull[ing] the strings", expressed support for the UK recognition of the Armenian genocide, and strongly urged the House to provide more assistance to the Armenian refugees.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-52)
In June 2015, she was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate Jeremy Corbyn as a candidate in the Labour leadership election,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman3-53) although she later supported Yvette Cooper.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph3-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman4-55)
Huq supported Owen Smith in his unsuccessful attempt to replace Corbyn in the 2016 Labour Party leadership election.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-56)

And so I would find it difficult to vote against somebody like that, and I hope that our people around the country are discriminating and think and act in a constructive way."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-chiswickherald2-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-spectator2-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph4-43) At the snap 2017 general election, Huq was re-elected as MP for Ealing Central and Acton with an increased vote share of 59.7% and an increased majority of 13,807 votes.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon7-47)
At the 2019 general election, Huq was again re-elected, with a decreased vote share of 51.3% and a decreased majority of 13,300 votes.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-48)

## Parliamentary career
Huq was appointed vice-chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Music Group and All-Party Parliamentary on Crossrail. She chairs the All-Party Parliamentary Group on London, with specific reference to planning and the built environment.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbwhoswho-15) In June 2020 Huq joined the Panel of Chairs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-49) She has been a member of the Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee since March 2022.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-50)
In August 2022, Huq was re-selected as the Labour candidate for Ealing Central and Acton at the 2024 general election.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-51)
In a debate with the UK Parliament House of Commons in March 2024, Huq recognized the expulsion of Armenians from Nagorno-Karabakh as ethnic cleansing, noted the erasure and destruction of Armenian churches and crosses, criticized the UK's dependency on oil for "pull[ing] the strings", expressed support for the UK recognition of the Armenian genocide, and strongly urged the House to provide more assistance to the Armenian refugees.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-52)
In June 2015, she was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate Jeremy Corbyn as a candidate in the Labour leadership election,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman3-53) although she later supported Yvette Cooper.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph3-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman4-55)
Huq supported Owen Smith in his unsuccessful attempt to replace Corbyn in the 2016 Labour Party leadership election.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-56)

## Parliamentary career
She nominated Keir Starmer as a candidate in the 2020 Labour leadership election.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-57)
In April 2016, Huq defended suspended Labour MP Naz Shah during an interview on BBC's _Today_ programme by comparing "alleged anti-Semitic" posts about Israel shared by Shah on social media to a photo Huq shared of Boris Johnson on a zip-wire next to Barack Obama. She also stressed the fact that Shah's comments were made before she became an MP and that some online comments should not be taken seriously. Subsequently, Huq was accused of "trivialising racism".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon5-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-Simons-59) Huq later apologised, saying she was not "fully aware" of Shah's comments before defending her.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-spectator1-60)
In April 2016, Huq claimed that some areas of television had yet to move forward from the racially insensitive sitcoms of the 1970s. She specifically criticised the BBC comedy _Citizen Khan_'s "Islamophobic" depiction of a "quite backward" family of Muslims. The BBC responded that "We've also had positive comments from members of the Muslim community for the show and for creator Adil Ray who, like the family portrayed, is a British Pakistani Muslim. As with all sitcoms the characters are comic creations and not meant to be representative of the community as a whole".[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbc3-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-theweek-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-birminghammail-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-expressandstar-64)

After the choral scholarship took him to Peterborough, he returned to London and studied law at the School of Oriental and African Studies. David Lammy's path from Tottenham to Harvard Law School is the kind of story that sounds almost unbelievable until you know the details. After the choral scholarship took him to Peterborough, he returned to London and studied law at the School of Oriental and African Studies. He was called to the Bar in 1994 at Lincoln's Inn and then, in 1997, he became the first Black Briton to study a master's in law at Harvard Law School, graduating that same year. He came back to London, practiced law, and in 2000, following the sudden death of legendary Tottenham MP Bernie Grant, he was selected as the Labour candidate for the seat. He was twenty-seven years old when he won and became one of the youngest MPs in Parliament at the time. He has represented Tottenham ever since. The constituency where he grew up, where his mother juggled three jobs, where he learned the particular texture of working-class life in a diverse inner-city community, became the place he chose to serve. There is something profoundly intentional about that. Nicola has been part of his life throughout the years of political growth, the long years in opposition, the Lammy Review in 2017 that exposed racial bias in the criminal justice system, and his appointment as Foreign Secretary in 2024 and then Deputy Prime Minister in 2025. Having a partner whose own work is about identity, representation, and bearing witness has clearly mattered to a politician whose whole career has been shaped by those same concerns.
